title: MDOT nominee on hold, Moore officially on ballot, Ellis is present, and not, more political notes
summary: The Transportation secretary nominee is put in a holding pattern in the Senate, the governor is officially on the ballot for 2026, and Sen. Arthur Ellis (D-Charles) wants to be counted as present, but not indicate his presence, plus more in political notes.
content:
by Bryan P. Sears, Maryland Matters February 23, 2026

by Bryan P. Sears, Maryland Matters February 23, 2026

Gov. Wes Moore’s nominee for Transportation secretary is in a holding pattern after a Senate confirmation hearing Monday.

Kathryn Thomson was one of two department secretaries to come before the Senate Executive Nominations Committee, where the former Federal Aviation Administration director faced questions about Baltimore City transportation projects.

But Senate President Bill Ferguson (D-Baltimore City) asked that Thomson’s nomination be pulled from a list of two-dozen that appeared before the committee Monday. He said the hold was at the request of the Baltimore City delegation, which had sent Thomson a letter inquiring about a transportation plan for the city, including specifics on BMore Bus Transit plan and the stalled Red Line light rail project.

“In my opinion, I think that the Baltimore region’s transit system has always been like an afterthought or a second child,” Sen. Cory McCray (D-Baltimore) said to Thomson during the hearing.

Both McCray and Ferguson asked about the bus transit plan. Ferguson also asked about the Red Line, which Moore relaunched in June of 2023 and vowed to be under construction as early as this year.

Ferguson added that he was concerned about “minuscule early investments” in the transit line and “zeroed out” funding for Red Line construction.

“I think there’s a generalized concern as we look towards how do people, goods and services move within the Baltimore region, that we were hopeful that we would see a much more robust investment in a real plan and vision for the Baltimore region,” Ferguson said during an exchange with Thomson. “It sounds like that’s not what is anticipated for this year.”

Ferguson said the delegation “was expecting a more robust response than was provided today, which was not a response at all. And so, we’d like to follow up to have additional conversations.”

All that was left was the paperwork.

And on Monday, Gov. Wes Moore (D) made his bid for a second term official.

“While Trump’s reckless policies cost Marylanders their jobs and raise prices on everything, here in Maryland we are showing across the state and party lines that there’s a better way forward to make our economy stronger and everyday life more affordable,” Moore said in a statement.

As of Monday, Moore was one of two Democrats filed for the primary. A third, perennial candidate Ralph Jaffe, is still listed as an active candidate. Jaffe died two weeks ago.

For those keeping score at home, Sen. Arthur Ellis (D-Charles) now wants to be counted in Senate quorum calls.

Kinda.

Three weeks ago, Ellis began a protest in which he said he would refuse to push a button registering his presence on the floor for the purposes of determining if the chamber had a quorum and could conduct business. Ellis said he would not registers his presence until a congressional redistricting bill is moved from the Rules Committee to the full Senate for a vote.

The protest was dubious to begin with since Democrats already make up two-thirds of the chamber — more than enough on their own to reach the magic number of 24 for a quorum. Additionally, rules governing the Senate state that if a legislator is present on the floor, they are counted toward the quorum, whether they register their presence or not.

For more than two weeks now, Ellis has refrained from pushing the button. But on Friday, Ellis stopped the Senate session to ask a question.

Senate President Bill Ferguson (D-Baltimore City) announced 40 senators present. Ellis appeared to feel left out.

“So, you said there are 40 members present,” Ellis said. “Since my protest is that I don’t quorum in, can you say 41 is present? You said earlier that my presence is being here.”

Ferguson agreed.

And on Monday night, as the Senate adjourned for the evening, 41 senators registered their presence. And Ellis was counted anyway with Ferguson noting “42 members present in the chamber.”

Senate Minority Leader Stephen S. Hershey Jr. (R-Upper Shore) said he nixed a potential run for governor after deciding the Senate was the best place to “fight for fiscally responsible policies, affordable energy, and strong local communities.”

Hershey announced last fall he was considering a run for governor and forming an exploratory committee after Ed Hale, a Baltimore businessman, announcing he was changing his party affiliation to seek the Republican nomination for governor. Hershey called Hale a political opportunist, and said he might also run.

But Friday, Hershey filed for re-election in his district. It’s a seat he has held since 2015.

“Maryland faces real challenges right now — from rising energy costs and affordability pressures to a budget that has been badly mismanaged,” Hershey told Maryland Matters. “Those battles are being fought in the legislature today, and they require experienced leadership willing to challenge one-party rule, demand accountability, and deliver real solutions.”

There’s no club for state officials with famous names, but if there were, John Marshall would have to be added to the roll.

Marshall, a recent appointee to the Criminal Justice Compensation Board, was one of two dozen nominees to come before the Senate Executive Nominations Committee Monday night. Marshall shares a name with another John Marshall, the fourth chief justice of the United State Supreme Court. Marshall presided over a number of key decisions including Marbury v. Madison, establishing the power of American courts to void laws and that violate the U.S. Constitution.

The namesake appointee impressed at least one senator.

“He’s an attorney. His name is John Marshall, chief justice of the United States. I’m loving this,” said Sen. William C. Smith Jr. (D-Montgomery), chair of the Senate Judicial Proceedings Committee. Smith, an attorney, attended the College of William and Mary, the alma mater of Justice Marshall.

“That’s a curse,” joked Marshall, the board appointee.

“Also, my name is Will Smith. I feel your pain,” Smith responded.
